node-1.label: An 80-year-old woman presented with difficulty raising her right upper limb, progressive dyskinesia, gait disorder, neck pain, and numbness in her extremities

node-2.label: She had neck pain for approximately 2 years and numbness in her extremities for about 1 year, both significantly worsened before her visit; she could walk unassisted for less than 100 meters

node-3.label: Physical examination showed muscle weakness (MMT score 3) in the entire right upper limb, normal strength in the remaining limbs, hypesthesia throughout the upper and lower limbs, increased deep tendon reflexes bilaterally in all limbs, positive Hoffman's and Wartenberg's signs, and preoperative JOA score 8.5 points

node-4.label: Radiographs and cervical contrast CT revealed osteolytic lesions in C3-7; a mass extended into the spinal canal from within the vertebrae, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side; the mass was stained in the early contrast phase and showed an internal low-density area; MRI detected a mass with the same signal profile as bone from within the C3-7 vertebrae to outside of the vertebral bodies, compressing the cervical spinal cord from the right side at the same levels

node-5.label: Blood tests showed no thrombocytopenia, anemia, or coagulation abnormalities; inflammatory response was normal; blood cultures and various tumor markers were negative; percutaneous vertebral biopsy showed culture negativity and no neoplastic lesions

attrs.why: Pathologist and Radiologist analyses concordantly support a neoplastic process rather than infection/inflammation or a non-neoplastic bone lesion. The biopsy shows atypical vasoforming proliferation with vascular markers, Ki-67 10.6–16.1%, and infiltration into surrounding muscle/fat, and imaging shows an osteolytic C3-7 mass with cord compression. This expert concordance raises confidence in cervical spine neoplasm from 0.80 to 0.82.

Pathologist explicitly states infection is unlikely and the vascular immunophenotype does not fit an infectious/inflammatory process; cultures and inflammatory markers were already negative. Confidence is decreased from 0.08 to 0.05.

Pathologist and Radiologist both state a non-neoplastic bone lesion is unlikely. The atypical vasoforming proliferation, vascular marker positivity, elevated Ki-67, and infiltration into muscle/fat refute a non-neoplastic lesion; confidence is decreased from 0.12 to 0.10.

node-9.label: Biopsy shows atypical vasoforming proliferation with ERG, CD31, and CD34 positivity

node-10.label: Biopsy shows pericytic markers myo1B, CD146, and SMA positivity and is negative for D2-40, CAMTA1, TFE3, and FOSB

node-11.label: Ki-67 proliferation index in biopsy is approximately 16.1% and 10.6%

node-12.label: Biopsy specimen shows infiltration into surrounding muscle and fat

attrs.why: Pathologist analysis explicitly favors a cervical spine vascular neoplasm and describes the biopsy as an atypical vasoforming proliferation with endothelial ERG/CD31/CD34 positivity and pericytic myo1B/CD146/SMA positivity. This direct concordance slightly increases confidence from 0.80 to 0.82.

node-14.label: Pathologist recommends tumor subtyping with oncology and spine surgery correlation

node-15.label: Radiologist recommends contrast-enhanced MRI/MRA to assess vascular supply and multidisciplinary management

node-16.label: Cervical spine vascular neoplasm with locally aggressive behavior

attrs.why: Pathologist emphasizes Ki-67 10.6–16.1% and infiltration into muscle/fat, which support locally aggressive behavior of the vascular neoplasm. Combined with the osteolytic C3-7 mass compressing the cord, confidence is increased from 0.65 to 0.68.

Pathologist analysis states angiosarcoma is the leading diagnosis, based on atypical vasoforming cells, ERG/CD31/CD34 positivity, myo1B/CD146/SMA-positive pericytes, Ki-67 10.6–16.1%, and infiltration into muscle/fat. These features support a malignant vascular neoplasm and refine the broad vascular neoplasm hypothesis. Confidence is increased from 0.35 to 0.62, but remains below certainty because MYC/TP53 molecular testing, resection details, molecular panel, HIV/HHV-8 status, and MRI/MRA are still missing.

Pathologist reports that negative EHE markers exclude epithelioid hemangioendothelioma. This is consistent with the already negative CAMTA1/TFE3 findings and directly lowers the likelihood of EHE as an alternative vascular subtype, reducing confidence from 0.18 to 0.05.

Vertebral hemangioma is the most common vascular lesion of the spine, and node-4 shows an osteolytic C3-7 mass with early-phase contrast staining; yet the biopsy atypia (node-9) and elevated Ki-67 (node-11) argue against a simple benign hemangioma, so this is a low-probability refinement of the frontier.
A vascular neoplasm that can arise in the spine and would fit the frontier, but node-10 shows D2-40 negativity and there is no VHL context, making hemangioblastoma a less likely fine-grained subtype.

A vascular tumor sharing endothelial marker positivity with the frontier, but HHV8 status is unknown and the clinical setting is atypical, so this is a rare possible subtype of the vascular neoplasm hypothesis.

Pathologist analysis states angiosarcoma is the leading diagnosis, based on atypical vasoforming cells, ERG/CD31/CD34 positivity, myo1B/CD146/SMA-positive pericytes, Ki-67 10.6–16.1%, and infiltration into muscle/fat. These features support a malignant vascular neoplasm and refine the broad vascular neoplasm hypothesis. Confidence is increased from 0.35 to 0.62, but remains below certainty because MYC/TP53 molecular testing, resection details, molecular panel, HIV/HHV-8 status, and MRI/MRA are still missing.

Pathologist reports that negative EHE markers exclude epithelioid hemangioendothelioma. This is consistent with the already negative CAMTA1/TFE3 findings and directly lowers the likelihood of EHE as an alternative vascular subtype, reducing confidence from 0.18 to 0.05.

Vertebral hemangioma is the most common vascular lesion of the spine, and node-4 shows an osteolytic C3-7 mass with early-phase contrast staining; yet the biopsy atypia (node-9) and elevated Ki-67 (node-11) argue against a simple benign hemangioma, so this is a low-probability refinement of the frontier.
A vascular neoplasm that can arise in the spine and would fit the frontier, but node-10 shows D2-40 negativity and there is no VHL context, making hemangioblastoma a less likely fine-grained subtype.

A vascular tumor sharing endothelial marker positivity with the frontier, but HHV8 status is unknown and the clinical setting is atypical, so this is a rare possible subtype of the vascular neoplasm hypothesis.

node-5.label: Blood tests showed no thrombocytopenia, anemia, or coagulation abnormalities; inflammatory response was normal; blood cultures and various tumor markers were negative; percutaneous vertebral biopsy showed culture negativity and no neoplastic lesions
